'''Leo Blitz''' (March 21, 1946 – December 20, 2022) was an American astronomer, researcher, and a professor of [[astronomy]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] (UC Berkeley).

== Early life ==
Blitz was born in [[Munich]] on March 21, 1946, although his birth certificate was later altered (to October 21, 1946)<ref name="nli">{{cite web |title=Blitz, Leo |url=https://www.nli.org.il/en/authorities/987007456166405171 |website=nli.org.il |publisher=[[National Library of Israel]] |access-date=20 August 2026 |archive-date=22 February 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250222060918/https://www.nli.org.il/en/authorities/987007456166405171 |url-status=live }}</ref> because, in order for his family to emigrate to the US, he needed to be older and a Polish citizen.<ref name="baas">{{cite journal |title=Leo Blitz (1945–2022) |journal=Bulletin of the AAS |date=2023 |volume=55 |issue=1 |url=https://doi.org/10.3847/25c2cfeb.008e4e7b |access-date=March 5, 2025}}</ref>

His mother Maria, who grew up in the [[Warsaw Ghetto]], survived [[Auschwitz]] and the [[Stutthof concentration camp]], and was one of only 30 survivors of the [[Yantarny, Kaliningrad Oblast#Massacre of Palmnicken|Palmnicken Massacre]]. She met and married Leo's father Abraham Blitz in Krakow in 1945. Abraham Blitz, who was born in Poland but grew up in [[Vienna]], was in Krakow serving in the occupying [[Soviet Army]].<ref name="baas"/>

== Career ==
Completing his [[Bachelor's degree|bachelor's]] from [[Cornell University]] in [[engineering physics]] in 1967, Blitz worked for six years as a [[Nuclear engineering|nuclear engineer]] on [[Power station|power plant]] safety. Between 1973 and 1976, he did his [[Master's degree|master's]] from [[Columbia University]] wherein he worked using a millimeter-wave [[telescope]] to map [[carbon monoxide]] (CO) around [[Rosette Nebula]] to find a [[giant molecular cloud]] (GMC).<ref name="ucb blitz">{{cite web |title=In Memoriam - Leo Blitz |url=https://senate.universityofcalifornia.edu/in-memoriam/files/leo-blitz.html |last=Heiles |first=Carl |website=senate.universityofcalifornia.edu |publisher=[[University of California]] |access-date=20 August 2026}}</ref> He later completed his postdoctorate also from Columbia University in 1979 with [[Patrick Thaddeus]] as his [[doctoral advisor]].<ref name="astrogen aau">{{cite web |title=Leo Blitz (1946 - 2022) |url=https://astrogen.aas.org/front/searchdetails.php?agnumber=9571 |website=astrogen.aas.org |publisher=[[American Astronomical Society]] |access-date=20 August 2026 |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230608150238/https://astro.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/leo_blitz_obituary_v1.6.pdf |archive-date=2023-06-08}}</ref><ref>Blitz, L. (1979). [https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1979PhDT.........4B/abstract A Study of the Molecular Complexes Accompanying MON OB1 MON OB2 and CMA OB1]. Ph. D. Thesis.</ref> Between 1978 and 1981 he was a postdoctoral fellow at the [[Radio Astronomy Laboratory]] at UC Berkeley.<ref name="sciam 1982">{{Cite web |url=https://sciam-cms.s3.amazonaws.com/sciam/cache/file/C74354C3-B029-48C8-BCC404CAF0BEB683.pdf |title=''Scientific American Magazine'', April 1982, Volume 246, Number 4, p. 15 |access-date=2026-08-20 |archive-date=2024-11-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241130070906/https://sciam-cms.s3.amazonaws.com/sciam/cache/file/C74354C3-B029-48C8-BCC404CAF0BEB683.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="iasedu">{{cite web |title=Past Member - Leo Blitz |url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/leo-blitz |website=www.ias.edu |publisher=[[Institute for Advanced Study]] |access-date=20 August 2026 |language=en |date=9 December 2019 |archive-date=19 March 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250319023454/https://www.ias.edu/scholars/leo-blitz |url-status=live }}</ref>

Starting in 1981, Blitz was appointed as a professor in the [[University of Maryland, College Park|University of Maryland College Park]] where he also researched on the [[star formation]] of GMCs.<ref name="sciam 1982" /><ref name="iasedu" /> From 1988 to 1996, he served as the director for [[millimeter-wave astronomy]] at UMB.<ref name="aas" /> Following which in 1996, he moved to the UC Berkeley where he became a director of the Radio Astronomy Laboratory<ref name="aas" /> and worked with the [[Berkeley-Illinois-Maryland Association]] (BIMA) telescope array. As a member of BIMA, a survey was conducted by Blitz called "Survey of Normal Galaxies" to find out about young GMCs and rate of its star formation that differed from [[galaxy]] to galaxy.<ref name="ucb blitz" /> Between 1994 and 1997, he also was a member of the [[National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine|National Research Council]] (NRC) Committee on [[Astronomy]] and [[Astrophysics]].<ref name="aas" />

Later from 2004, Blitz was working with [[Combined Array for Research in Millimeter-wave Astronomy]]'s (CARMA) telescopes which was developed by combining three different telescope designs from two university [[Radio observatory|radio observatories]] and BIMA.<ref name="carma ucb">{{cite web |last1=Sanders |first1=Bob |title=New CARMA radio telescope array will combine UC Berkeley, Caltech arrays |url=https://newsarchive.berkeley.edu/news/media/releases/2004/03/29_carma.shtml |website=newsarchive.berkeley.edu |publisher=[[University of California, Berkeley]] |access-date=20 August 2026 |archive-date=17 April 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260417093608/https://newsarchive.berkeley.edu/news/media/releases/2004/03/29_carma.shtml |url-status=live }}</ref> This work led Blitz to take up another survey project, [[Atlas 3d survey]], to observe 30 galaxies for detecting CO using CARMA. He also was a professor of astronomy at the UC Berkeley and later became its [[emeritus professor]].<ref name="ucb blitz" />

As a member of [[International Astronomical Union]] (IAU), Blitz served as the president of Commission 33 Structure & Dynamics of the Galactic System and IAU's different divisions.<ref name="iau">{{cite web |title=Leo Blitz (1946 - 2022) United States |url=https://www.iau.org/IAU/Shared_Content/Contacts/ContactLayouts/Obituary.aspx?ID=26144 |website=iau.org |publisher=[[International Astronomical Union]] |access-date=20 August 2026}}</ref> He also served as the [[councillor]] of [[American Astronomical Society]] (AAS) from 1995 to 1998 and also in its Warner/Pierce Prize Committee from 2002 to 2003.<ref name="aas">{{cite web |title=Candidate Statement: Leo Blitz |url=https://aas.org/candidate-statement-leo-blitz |website=aas.org |publisher=[[American Astronomical Society]] |access-date=20 August 2026 |archive-date=22 February 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250222095020/https://aas.org/candidate-statement-leo-blitz |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2006, [[Martin D. Weinberg]], professor of astronomy at the [[University of Massachusetts Amherst]], worked with Blitz to create a computer model to observe an obscure warp of the [[Magellanic Clouds]] in the [[Milky Way Galaxy]]. On the phenomenon, Blitz remarked that "it looks like the Milky Way is flapping in the breeze".<ref>{{cite web |last1=Cain |first1=Fraser |title=How the Milky Way Got its Warp |url=https://www.universetoday.com/articles/how-the-milky-way-got-its-warp |website=universetoday.com |publisher=[[Universe Today]] |access-date=20 August 2026 |language=en |date=9 January 2006 |archive-date=14 May 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260514022040/https://www.universetoday.com/articles/how-the-milky-way-got-its-warp |url-status=live }}</ref>

Between 2006 and 2008, Blitz was the director of the [[Allen Telescope Array|Allen Telescopic Array]] (ATA).<ref name="aas" /> On October 16, 2007, the first forty-two [[radio dish]]es of the ATA were launched to collect scientific data on far distances in the [[universe]]. ATA was made by a joint collaboration between UC Berkeley, of whom Blitz was one of its representatives, and the [[SETI Institute]].<ref name="astromag">{{cite web |title=Allen Telescope Array begins |url=https://www.astronomy.com/science/allen-telescope-array-begins/ |website=astronomy.com |publisher=Astronomy (magazine) |access-date=20 August 2026 |date=16 October 2007 |archive-date=10 June 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260610091209/https://www.astronomy.com/science/allen-telescope-array-begins/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2013, Blitz recognized the potential of a technique, known as [[Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array]] (ALMA), to measure large masses of black holes at farther distances.<ref name="ucb research">{{cite web |last1=Sanders |first1=Robert |title=Unmasking galaxies' hidden black holes |url=https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/news/unmasking-galaxies-hidden-black-holes |website=vcresearch.berkeley.edu |publisher=[[University of California, Berkeley]] |access-date=20 August 2026 |language=en |archive-date=29 July 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260729103140/https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/news/unmasking-galaxies-hidden-black-holes |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Davis |first1=Timothy A. |last2=B. |first2=Martin |last3=Cappellari |first3=Michele |last4=Sarzi |first4=Marc |last5=Blitz |first5=Leo |title=A black-hole mass measurement from molecular gas kinematics in NGC4526 |journal=Nature |date=February 2013 |volume=494 |issue=7437 |pages=328–330 |doi=10.1038/nature11819 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature11819 |access-date=20 August 2026 |archive-date=8 December 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241208050204/https://www.nature.com/articles/nature11819 |url-status=live |arxiv=1301.7184 }}</ref> An year later, Blitz, among one of the astronomers, found out five stars ([[Cepheid variable]]) at a distance of 75,000 [[light-year]]s away from [[Earth]]. He remarked that it was a challenging task as the thick dust blocks the light from any distant star.<ref name="sn">{{cite news |last1=Crockett |first1=Christopher |title=Milky Way's far side reveals some secrets |url=https://www.sciencenews.org/article/milky-ways-far-side-reveals-some-secrets |access-date=20 August 2026 |work=Astronomy |publisher=[[Science News]] |date=14 May 2014 |archive-date=12 December 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251212125937/https://www.sciencenews.org/article/milky-ways-far-side-reveals-some-secrets |url-status=live }}</ref>

As a professor, a total of 15 students including [[Nia Imara]] completed their [[Doctorate|postdoctorate]] under Blitz at the UC Berkeley.<ref name="astrogen aau" /><ref name="ucb blitz" />

== Personal life ==
Blitz was involved in various [[recreational activities]], including playing [[Squash (sport)|squash]], [[tennis]], [[bicycling]], [[fishing]], and [[running]]. He also listened to [[opera]], music, and enjoyed having good food especially [[gourmet chocolate]].<ref name="ucb blitz" />

Suffering from [[Parkinson's disease]] for a long time, Blitz died in his home in his family's presence on December 20, 2022, in [[Sonora, California]]. At the time, he was living with his wife, Lidewij de Vries, and his two sons and grandsons. He also has a sibling, Andrew.<ref name="ucb blitz" /><ref>{{cite news |title=Leo Blitz Obituary |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/nytimes/name/leo-blitz-obituary?id=38457078 |access-date=20 August 2026 |work=legacy.com |publisher=[[New York Times]] |date=23 December 2022}}</ref>
